# Payoneer alternatives in Nigeria

Compare 8 Payoneer alternatives in Africa on account features, market availability, virtual cards and fees

**Key takeaways**

- Payoneer is used for international payments, but account features and functionality varies by market
- WorldFirst offers multi-currency business accounts with 15+ currencies, marketplace collections, and up to 20 free virtual cards
- PayPal provides checkout, invoicing, and payment tools, but it is limited to send-only personal accounts in Nigeria and receive-only business accounts in Kenya and Morocco, with no cards
- Grey offers USD accounts with sending, receiving, and virtual cards, but business accounts are only available in Nigeria
- Eversend provides USD/EUR accounts, transfers, and virtual cards, but card usage comes with monthly or per-card fees starting at US$1
- nSave provides multi-currency accounts, but GBP accounts in Nigeria cannot receive funds

Payoneer is a global payments provider that helps freelancers, online sellers, and businesses receive international payments, collect marketplace payouts, and send funds worldwide. For businesses in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and Morocco, account features and pricing differ meaningfully across providers. This guide compares 8 alternatives to Payoneer across these markets.

## 1. WorldFirst

WorldFirst is a global payments provider that helps businesses receive, hold, convert, and send international payments through a single multi-currency account. The World Account allows businesses to open local currency accounts in more than 15 currencies including USD, EUR, GBP, CNH, AUD, and NZD.

Businesses can also collect payouts from multiple global marketplaces and payment gateways. Each account is also linked to a virtual card called the [World Card](https://www.worldfirst.com/af/product/pay/world-card/) that provides virtual Mastercard access with up to 20 virtual cards available at no additional cost.

| Key features | Open local bank account details in 15+ currencies, including USD, GBP, EUR, CNH, AUD and NZDCollect payments from 130+ global marketplaces and payment gateways, including Amazon, Etsy and StripeSend and receive payments in 100+ currencies across 200+ countries and regionsFree and instant payments between World Account holdersUse Xero or NetSuite integration to reconcile transactions |
| --- | --- |
| Main fees | **Monthly fee:** Zero   **Opening virtual local currency accounts:** Zero   **Receiving payments:** Zero   **Holding funds in multiple currencies:** Zero   **Sending payments:** Refer to in-portal pricing. Vouchers may apply   **Currency conversion:** Refer to in-portal pricing. Vouchers may apply   **Getting a World Card:** Zero up to 20 cards |

**Fees checked in June 2026. Terms and Conditions Apply.*

[Open a World Account](https://portal.worldfirst.com/register?lang=en-GB&region=AF)

## 2. PayPal

PayPal is an international payments provider used for sending and receiving money for businesses and individuals across 200+ countries and 25+ currencies.1 Personal accounts are limited to sending payments, while business accounts support both sending and receiving.2,4

PayPal Nigeria only has personal accounts with send-only functionality4, while Kenya and Morocco support business accounts that are receive-only.2,3 Ghana is currently not supported.

→ For more details, read our [PayPal review](https://www.worldfirst.com/af/blog/business-banking-insights/paypal-business-nigeria-morocco-kenya/) and compare it with PayPal alternatives

**Pricing**: No monthly fee.5 Businesses receiving payments pay 4.40% plus a fixed transaction fee6

## 3. Wise

Wise enables international transfers in 50+ currencies to over 140 countries.6 Personal accounts are available in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and Morocco, but are restricted to sending payments only.7

Wise Business is available in Kenya but it is send-only.8

**Pricing**: No account opening fee. Transfer fees vary by currency and payment route, starting from 0.29%9

## 4. Grey

Grey is an international payment provider that offers both personal and business accounts with USD virtual account details.10 “Personal accounts support receiving, sending and exchanging currencies, and include a virtual card for spending11. Business accounts come with more features like bulk payouts, team spending controls, and API access.10

Personal accounts are accessible in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and Morocco14,15,16, while business accounts are limited to Nigeria only.10 Grey offers virtual cards at an issuance cost starting at US$4.13

→ For more details, read our [Grey review](https://www.worldfirst.com/af/blog/business-banking-insights/grey-review-africa/) and compare it with Grey alternatives

**Pricing**: No monthly fee.10 Receiving fees varies as per transaction type–0.8% for ACH, SEPA and FPS12

## 5. Eversend

Eversend provides USD and EUR virtual accounts along with USD virtual cards.17

Its business accounts mirror the core personal account features but add API access for automating payment processes.18 The platform is available for both personal and business users in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana.19 Morocco is not currently supported.

**Pricing**: Account opening costs US$2. Transfers incur a 0.7% fee21 Virtual cards either come with a US$1 monthly maintenance fee or a one-time US$3 per card charge.20

## 6. Chipper Cash

Chipper Cash is a cross-border payments provider, offering USD virtual accounts and USD virtual cards for global spending in 21 countries.22

Personal accounts are limited to sending money only, whereas business accounts support both sending and receiving funds, and come with higher transaction limits, and dedicated enterprise support.23 USD virtual cards come with issuance and maintenance fees starting from US$1.25

Chipper Cash is currently available in Nigeria and Ghana.23

→ For more details, read our [Chipper Cash review](https://www.worldfirst.com/af/blog/business-banking-insights/chipper-cash-review/) and compare it with [Chipper Cash alternatives](https://www.worldfirst.com/af/blog/business-banking-insights/chipper-cash-review/)

**Pricing**: Both business and personal accounts come at zero cost24, but USD virtual accounts require a setup fee of NGN 5,000 / GHS 60 and a US$1.50 monthly fee26

## 7. Remitly

Remitly operates as a money transfer service rather than a multi-currency account.27 It is used for cross-border payments and does not provide personal or business accounts.

Businesses in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and Morocco can receive funds through bank deposits, cash pickup, or mobile money depending on the country.28,29,30,31

**Pricing:** No monthly/set up fee27

## 8. nSave

nSave provides multi-currency business accounts that let companies receive international payments in USD, EUR, and GBP, while also enabling them to hold balances, send money overseas, and convert between supported currencies.32 It also includes virtual card access for business spending.34

The service is available for business use in Nigeria, Kenya, and Morocco.33 GBP accounts in Nigeria cannot receive incoming funds.35

**Pricing36**: Business accounts have a one-time setup fee of US$10. Sending GBP payments costs US$1 per transaction, while USD and EUR SWIFT transfers cost 0.3% (minimum US$14.99 and maximum US$24.99)

## Choose the right Payoneer alternative

When comparing Payoneer alternatives, availability can be just as important as pricing or features. Some providers focus on specific countries, while others offer different functionality depending on where a business is based. Before choosing a platform, it is worth checking whether you can not only open an account, but also receive payments, hold balances, access cards, and manage multiple currencies in the markets where your business operates.

[Open a World Account](https://portal.worldfirst.com/register?lang=en-GB&region=AF)

## FAQs

### Which is the best alternative to Payoneer for African businesses?

The best alternative is one that is available across Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and Morocco and offers business account functionality, multi-currency support, virtual cards, and competitive fees.

### Does Payoneer charge a monthly fee?

No. Payoneer does not currently charge a monthly account fee, although other transaction and service fees may apply.

### Can Payoneer be used to receive payments?

Yes. Payoneer allows businesses and freelancers to receive international payments from clients, marketplaces, and payment platforms. You can know more about the platform on our Payoneer review.

### Which Payoneer alternatives offer a multi-currency card?

WorldFirst offers the World Card, a virtual Mastercard linked to its multi-currency account, allowing businesses to spend in multiple currencies and create up to 20 virtual cards at no extra cost.

pages.title: How Digital Payments Are Transforming Businesses in Nigeria • Channels Television
pages.text:
# How Digital Payments Are Transforming Businesses in Nigeria • Channels Television

**If you live in Nigeria today, you already feel it! Money now moves more by phone than by hand. Nigerians pay for groceries, transport, rent, and even school fees with instant transfers. Young Nigerians now use different digital tools, from a [forex trading app](https://www.hfm.com/int/en-ng/platforms/mobile-application) for side investments to instant transfers and mobile wallets for everyday spending.**

This change is not just a feeling. It is backed by hard numbers released in the last few months.

On 3 July 2025, reports noted that Nigeria processed 7.9 billion real-time transactions in 2024, based on data from EnterpriseNGR. That made Nigeria Africa’s leading real-time payments market and placed it among global leaders like India, Brazil, and Thailand. Those 7.9 billion payments represented 2.97% of the entire world’s 266.2 billion real-time transactions in 2024.

Read Also

- [WTO Warns Of ‘Most Serious And Sustained’ Trade Disruptions›](https://www.channelstv.com/2026/09/15/wto-warns-of-most-serious-and-sustained-trade-disruptions/?utm_source=auto-read-also&utm_medium=web)
- [US, Canada Unable To Reach Trade Pact To Avert Trump Tariffs›](https://www.channelstv.com/2026/08/22/us-canada-unable-to-reach-trade-pact-to-avert-trump-tariffs/?utm_source=auto-read-also&utm_medium=web)
- [Brazil Seeks WTO Consultation Over US Tariffs›](https://www.channelstv.com/2026/07/28/brazil-seeks-wto-consultation-over-us-tariffs/?utm_source=auto-read-also&utm_medium=web)

Real-time payments sit inside a much bigger cashless story. On 29 July 2025, new reports citing fresh NIBSS data showed that electronic payment transactions hit ₦284.99 trillion in Q1 2025. That was a 17.7% increase over the ₦234.49 trillion recorded in Q1 2024. Point-of-sale (PoS) payments alone reached ₦10.45 trillion in that same quarter, more than double the ₦3.62 trillion seen a year earlier.

The report also highlighted how quickly PoS terminals are spreading. In January 2025, there were 5.5 million active PoS terminals in Nigeria. By March 2025, that number had risen to 5.9 million. In the same months of 2024, only about 2.4–2.6 million terminals were active. That means more physical touchpoints for digital money in markets, motor parks, and small shops.

The growth is not only in one quarter. NIBSS data, summarised in an August 2025 insight note, showed that total electronic payments in Nigeria reached around ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2024, the highest level ever recorded. Another analysis of the same NIBSS figures noted that about 11.2 billion e-payment transactions were processed in 2024, a rise of more than 15% year-on-year.

Real-time rails are doing most of the heavy lifting. A payment trends review published in June 2025 using ACI Worldwide data found that NIBSS Instant Payments (NIP), launched back in 2011, accounted for 82.1% of all cashless transactions in Nigeria in 2023. It also estimated that 27.7% of all transactions in the country in 2023 were real-time payments, and projected that this share could reach 50.1% by 2028.

This growth is now being recognised at a continental level. In November 2025, AfricaNenda’s SIIPS 2025 work cited NIP as Africa’s first “mature” instant payment system, and highlighted that instant payments across Africa altogether reached nearly US$2 trillion in value in 2024, with Nigeria as a major contributor.

The macroeconomic impact is also being measured. A December 2024 analysis of Nigeria and South Africa’s real-time payments estimated that in 2023, real-time payments added around US$7 billion to Nigeria’s GDP. It is projected that this contribution could grow to US$15 billion by 2028, assuming adoption continues to deepen. For policymakers and investors, this is no longer just “fintech hype”. It is a measurable part of growth.

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) leaders recently shared updated data. At Nigeria Fintech Week 2025 in Lagos, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), through a representative of Olayemi Cardoso, said that electronic payment volumes increased from 3.9 billion (valued at ₦280 trillion) in August 2024 to 4.12 billion (valued at ₦384 trillion) by July 2025, reflecting growing adoption of digital payment channels

The social side of this shift is visible. More Nigerians now hold formal bank or wallet accounts. NIBSS reported in August 2025 that BVN-linked bank account holders had reached 66.2 million, and that total cashless transaction values had grown from ₦237.11 trillion in Q1 2024 to ₦295 trillion in Q1 2025. That means more people are inside the formal system, able to receive transfers, credits, and remittances directly.

Of course, this path is not smooth. The same NIBSS and media data that celebrate growth also hint at stress points. When monthly breakdowns of NIP usage show dips, like the fall from ₦100.06 trillion in January 2025 to ₦88.87 trillion in February before a recovery in March, analysts link part of this to network pressures and seasonal effects. Nigerians know the lived reality behind those numbers: queues at PoS stands when networks fail, and merchants holding goods while “awaiting alert”.

There are also fraud concerns. As transaction volumes rise into the hundreds of trillions of naira, banks and regulators repeatedly warn the public about fake alerts, phishing links, and social-engineering scams.

The rapid growth in real-time transactions, while positive, leaves less time to detect suspicious activity before money moves. This is why stronger authentication, better user education, and tighter monitoring are recurring themes at fintech conferences and CBN forums. Still, the direction of travel is clear.

In 2023, just over a quarter of Nigeria’s transactions were real-time. By 2028, it may be half. In 2024, Nigeria handled 7.9 billion real-time payments and more than a quadrillion naira in e-payments overall. In Q1 2025 alone, the country processed nearly ₦285 trillion electronically, with PoS volumes more than doubling year-on-year. These are not abstract figures. They describe how Nigerians now pay, save, send, and receive money.

For ordinary citizens, the benefits are straightforward: faster payments, more choice, and often more safety than carrying cash. For businesses, especially SMEs, real-time settlement can improve cash flow and reduce operational risk. For the wider economy, the data now show a clear link between real-time payments and GDP.

There is still work to do. Infrastructure must keep up. Fraud controls must tighten. Regulations need to protect users without killing innovation. But the last 12–18 months of data tell a consistent story: Nigeria is moving steadily toward a cash-light economy, and real-time payments are at the centre of that shift.

pages.text:
# PSV2025

## Payments System Vision 2025

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) launched and officially presented to the public the Payments System Vision 2025 (PSV 2025) on November 24, 2022. The Vision provides a five-year strategic roadmap for the Nigeria payments system to strengthen adoption of electronic payment, enhance safety, reliability and resilience of the system, account for new products and participants, foster financial inclusion and catalyse Nigeria's economic growth and development.

The emerging payments initiatives and schemes identified to achieve the above objectives are captured in the PSV 2025 with 10 (ten) key recommendations highlighted below to further facilitate the following objectives:

1. The CBN will review the core payments infrastructure and switching platform to ensure continued capability to meet payments demand. The potentials for Request for Payment (RfP) schemes will also be reviewed and the deployment of contactless solutions, contactless cards, and quick response code etc will be facilitated.
2. Create Open Banking roadmap for Nigeria, define a library of APIs supported by local market and consider the implementation of a regulatory sandbox that is appropriate for the Nigerian market.
3. Drive Agent Banking initiative and support the industry to explore solution that aid financial inclusion to accelerate the availability of basic banking and financial services to the unbanked.
4. Explore Blockchain solution such as Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) for the Naira, monitor the deployment of Blockchain solutions and the potentials for "Smart Contract" solutions in other countries to develop strategy for their possible adoption in Nigeria.
5. Develop a regulatory framework for potential implementation of "Stable Coins", and work with Securities & Exchange Commission to jointly develop regulatory framework for Initial Coin Offerings (ICO) in the event of the adoption of ICO-based investment solution in Nigeria.
6. Identify use cases for Big Data that has potential access to data in the payments system as well as support economic analysis.
7. Review the minimum-security requirements for banks to ensure they reflect the current industry best practices. The payments system architecture will also be reviewed to ensure that the minimum standards for user authentication are included as part of a multi-layer security solution.
8. Continue to support the use of Bank Verification Number (BVN) as an effective tool to check fraud in addition to exploring more potential use of BVN.
9. Request banks to strengthen consumer protection by issuing minimum required standards for swifter dispute resolution in Nigeria.
10. Interoperability shall continue to be a core principle of payments system in Nigeria. The tests to ensure compliance and license renewal, shall continue to form part of periodic assessment of Payments Service Providers.

### **OVERSIGHT**

In its effort to strengthen the oversight of the payments system, the Bank established the Oversight and Compliance Division (OCD) in the Payments System Management Department for effective monitoring of existing and planned payments system.  
The OCD activities include but are not limited to monitoring and oversight functions (onsite and offsite) on the payments system in Nigeria with particular reference to functions of Card and Payment Schemes (Schemes) Switching and Processing Companies (Switches), Mobile Money Operators (MMOs), Payment Terminals Service Providers (PTSPs), Payments Solution Service Providers (PSSPs), Payment Terminal Service Aggregators (PTSAs) and other Payment Service Providers.  
In this regard, the Bank has issued various licences to Payment Service Providers for operation in the Nigerian payments system.

pages.title: Fintech Laws and Regulations 2026 | Nigeria
pages.text:
# Fintech Laws and Regulations 2026

## **Approaches and developments**

The financial technology (“**Fintech**”) industry in Nigeria experienced remarkable growth in 2025 through 2026. As of March 2026, the number of Fintech startups in Nigeria has risen to over 500,[[i]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn1) from 233 in 2024.[[ii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn2) In 2025, Nigerian Fintech companies raised $230 million, which is 40% lower than the $410 million raised in 2024.[[iii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn3) Despite this decline, there has been increased government support for startups through programmes like the $50 million Impact Innovation Fund[[iv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn4) and the iDICE Startup Bridge.[[v]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn5)

The year 2025 also witnessed exciting acquisitions in the Nigerian Fintech space, with Fintech companies making cross-border and cross-sector acquisitions. Nigerian-founded cross-border payments company LemFi [acquired](https://techpoint.africa/insight/techpoint-digest-1018/) Irish currency exchange platform Bureau Buttercrane in January 2025.[[vi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn6) This acquisition granted LemFi an Irish licence and allowed it to deepen its financial services infrastructure and operate across the entire European Economic Area. Similarly, Bankly, a Nigerian Fintech company and licensed microfinance bank, [was acquired](https://businessday.ng/news/article/c-one-acquires-bankly-to-strengthen-fintech-footprint-in-nigeria/) by investment firm C-One.[[vii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn7) Nigerian digital asset startup Roqqu executed its East African expansion plan by [acquiring](http://startupresearcher.com/news/roqqu-acquires-flitaa) Flitaa, a Kenyan-based crypto platform.[[viii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn8)

In 2025, the Nigerian Fintech industry experienced regulatory reforms that are aimed at supporting innovation in the market. The Central Bank of Nigeria (“**CBN**”) recently released the Agent Banking Guidelines[[ix]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn9) to consolidate, amend and replace the Guidelines for the Regulation of Agent Banking and Agent Banking Relationships in Nigeria 2013 and the Regulatory Framework for Licensing Super-Agents in Nigeria 2015. One of the key changes in the Agent Banking Guidelines is that agents are only permitted to undertake agent banking services for one principal for a specified period. Open Banking in Nigeria also went live in August 2025, allowing for data sharing between banks and non-bank financial institutions. The CBN also reiterated to licensed financial operators that ISO 20022 is the required framework for payments and settlement communications in Nigeria, in line with both previous CBN directives and SWIFT’s international migration timeline, with the goal of ensuring consistent, high-quality data across Nigeria’s payments system.[[x]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn10) Also, following the success of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (“**PAPSS**”) in facilitating settlement of cross-border transactions within Africa, the CBN reviewed the documentation requirements for PAPSS transactions in Nigeria in April 2025.[[xi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn11) For Fintechs, PAPSS means instant, low-cost, cross-border payments in local African currencies.

Additionally, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (“**FCCPC**”) issued the Digital, Electronic, Online, or Non-traditional Consumer Lending Regulations 2025 (“**DEON Regulations**”) and the Digital, Electronic, Online, or Non-traditional Consumer Lending Guidelines 2025 (“**DEON Guidelines**”), which established a regulatory framework for the provision of digital and electronic consumer lending services in Nigeria. Another key regulatory development is that the Investment and Securities Act, 2025 (“**ISA 2025**”) now formally recognises digital and virtual assets as securities.[[xii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn12) As a result, entities involved in digital or virtual asset-related services are required to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“**SEC**”).

## **Fintech offering in Nigeria**

Fintech offerings in Nigeria may be classified into five major categories: (i) digital banking; (ii) alternative lending and digital credit; (iii) electronic payments; (iv) investment and financial management/crowdfunding; and (v) blockchain and digital currencies. These categories are further discussed below.

### **Digital banking**

Digital banking transforms the way people manage their finances by providing seamless, on-demand access to essential services, from transferring funds and paying bills to monitoring accounts, all through an intuitive digital platform, free from the constraints of traditional branch-based banking. By late 2025, the number of deployed Point-of-Sale (“**POS**”) devices had increased significantly from 155,000 in 2017 to roughly 8,400,000.[[xiii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn13) This growth has been driven by sustained consumer preference for digital channels and continued expansion of agency banking network across rural and semi-urban areas.

Also, the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (“**NIBSS**”) reported continued growth in electronic payment transactions and NIBSS Instant payment transactions, reinforcing the dominance of real-time payments within the financial ecosystem. The CBN noted that close to 11 billion transactions were processed in 2025, up from 5 billion transactions in 2022, placing the country among the top adopters globally and a clear leader on the African continent.[[xiv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn14) Following the continuous growth of digital banking, the CBN has also intensified its cashless policy initiatives and strengthened regulatory controls on electronic payment channels, including stricter Know-Your-Customer (“**KYC**”) requirements and enhanced monitoring of agent banking operations to mitigate fraud risks.[[xv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn15)

### **Alternative lending and digital credit**

Tech-driven alternative lending and direct credit platforms continue to bridge the credit gap in Nigeria by offering credit services through websites and mobile applications. These platforms provide customers with swift access to unsecured credit facilities online, which are more convenient for borrowers when compared to borrowing from traditional commercial banks. This is due to the reduced documentation requirements and the absence of a requirement for collateral in most cases. Operators in this space use machine-learning algorithms to perform real-time assessments of the creditworthiness of a user and to carry out risk evaluations of the ability of users to repay the loans. The algorithms usually rely on non-traditional digital data mined from the mobile phone of the user in the first instance, and credit report/history obtained from facilitators such as the credit bureaux (where available) for subsequent disbursements.

With the recent approval from the CBN for the launch of open banking in Nigeria, access to finance is set to receive a big boost as its implementation essentially allows regulated financial institutions to begin sharing financial data of customers amongst themselves, which began in August 2025.[[xvi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn16) Credit platforms can utilise customer data across bank accounts in determining the credit worthiness of the customer before advancing a loan. There is also a rise in “Buy Now Pay Later” (“**BNPL**”) products in Nigeria. BNPL products essentially allow customers to purchase goods and services upfront while deferring payments through convenient, scheduled instalment payments. The BNPL market in the country has experienced robust growth from 2022–2025, achieving a Compound Annual Growth Rate (“**CAGR**”) of 25.9%. This upward trajectory is expected to continue, with the market forecast to grow at a CAGR of 16.1% from 2026–2031.[[xvii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn17)

The FCCPC introduced the DEON Regulations on July 24, 2025[[xviii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn18) and the DEON Guidelines on November 18, 2025.[[xix]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn19) The DEON Regulations and DEON Guidelines govern unsecured loans delivered through digital or non-traditional channels, including airtime, cash, and cashback, and apply to all parties that earn or intend to earn revenue from such lending services, whether directly or indirectly. Following the April 2026 compliance deadline with the DEON Regulations, the FCCPC is now actively removing non-compliant lenders from its register and restricting their operations through app stores and payment providers. This clearly shows that the industry is in a period of consolidation and stricter compliance standards.

While this is expected to boost consumer trust and market stability, smaller or newer Fintechs may face higher costs and tougher entry barriers. Already, lenders have started to move away from nano loans as these loans were formerly accompanied by crass enforcement mechanisms and data privacy breaches.[[xx]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn20) The DEON Regulations now operate to strip that away. Nonetheless, the digital lending and alternative credit sector continues to witness systemic growth and increase. As of April 2026, the FCCPC has granted full approval to[492 digital lenders](https://fccpc.gov.ng/registration-of-digital-money-lenders/) in Nigeria,[[xxi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn21) a 13.62% increase from the 425 companies granted approval as of May 2025.[[xxii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn22) It is important to note, however, that the Federal High Court recently granted an interim injunction restraining the enforcement of the DEON Regulations. Pending the determination of the proceedings, the FCCPC would not be taking any steps in respect of the DEON Regulations.[[xxiii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn23)

### **Electronic payments**

As Nigeria descends further into a cashless economy, the value of electronic payments continues to rise. According to the CBN’s Q3 Bullion Report, electronic payment transactions surpassed ₦256 billion in total value in the third quarter of 2025, marking a 17.7% increase year-on-year growth from 2024.[[xxiv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn24) This surge was largely driven by the growing use of instant payment platforms, mobile banking services, Unstructured Supplementary Service Data, and POS terminals across the country. Agent Banking has greatly increased following the setting up of the Shared Agent Network Expansion Facility (“**SANEF**”), which has made electronic payments more accessible to underserved and underreached areas. Similarly, as of September 2025, Nigerian banks earned ₦514.82 billion ($356.91 million) from electronic payments.[[xxv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn25)

Foreign exchange and remittance transactions form part of the broader electronic payments landscape. The CBN’s regulatory oversight in this area is primarily anchored on two instruments: the Guidelines on International Mobile Money Remittance Service issued in 2014; and the Reviewed Guidelines on International Money Transfer Services in Nigeria published in 2024 (“**Reviewed Guidelines**”). Together, these frameworks authorise licensed operators to offer inbound international money remittance services within the country. Notably, the Reviewed Guidelines bar banks and Fintechs from applying for an International Money Transfer Operator (“**IMTO**”) licence, limiting their participation to an agency role, though the guidelines do not expressly address the status of banks and Fintechs that already hold an IMTO licence.[[xxvi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn26)

On the performance side, remittance inflows into Nigeria through licensed IMTOs declined in 2025 when measured against the comparable period in the prior year. According to CBN data, total IMTO inflows between January to September 2025 came in at approximately $3.22 billion, reflecting an 18.63% drop from the $3.82 billion recorded in the same period in 2024.[[xxvii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn27) Throughout this period, operators functioned under the Revised Regulations introduced by the CBN in 2024, which abolished fixed exchange rate ceilings and tightened oversight of remittance settlement processes. Recently, the CBN directed all licensed operators to open and maintain naira settlement accounts with banks and ensure that all transactions are routed strictly through these designated settlement accounts.[[xxviii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn28) This directive represents a notable tightening of the remittance regulatory landscape, plugging loopholes that had previously enabled funds to flow through less transparent channels, while further cementing the CBN’s broader drive to funnel foreign exchange inflows into the formal financial system.

### **Investment and financial management/crowdfunding**

Fintech platforms are increasingly broadening participation in financial markets, opening up access to equities, mutual funds, fixed income instruments, and international investment opportunities to a wider segment of the population. In 2025, domestic retail investors poured over ₦3.65 billion into equities listed on the Nigerian Exchange,[[xxix]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn29) marking a striking 56% jump compared to the ₦2.31 trillion recorded in the same period of 2024.[[xxx]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn30) This hike in participation is driven by platforms like Bamboo, Risevest, Cowrywise, Trove, and Chaka.[[xxxi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn31) Since the SEC began granting digital sub-broker licences in 2021, the sector has seen a growth in retail participation. Also, the Nigerian Stock Exchange has adopted Fintech solutions in the form of an automated trading system for securities trading on its floor.

Crowdfunding platforms are not in short supply, as Nigeria currently boasts of 111 crowdfunding startups in Nigeria.[[xxxii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn32) Crowdfunding has emerged as a significant source of financing for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (“**MSMEs**”) in Nigeria, particularly in sectors such as education, entertainment, manufacturing, and real estate. Unlike traditional equity or debt financing, it leverages online platforms to pool funds from a broad base of contributors toward a specific business, project, or venture.[[xxxiii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn33) In January 2021, the SEC introduced its Rules on Crowdfunding, establishing a regulatory framework under which eligible private companies can raise capital from the public through online crowdfunding platforms. A central feature of the Rules is the crowdfunding portal, which serves as the interface connecting fundraisers with potential investors. All crowdfunding intermediaries, including portal operators, are required to register with the SEC. The ISA 2025 has expanded the category of entities permitted to issue securities to the public by incorporating crowdfunding platforms through the inclusion of entities licensed by the CBN to accept deposits and savings from the public.[[xxxiv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn34) In addition, the ISA 2025 provides that an invitation to the public for the deposit of money with a person (including a Fintech entity) is subject to the written consent of the SEC and such invitation can only be made in accordance with the conditions and restrictions imposed by the SEC.[[xxxv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn35)

Robo advisors provide automated financial planning and investment services with little or no human supervision. In August 2021, the SEC issued its rules on Robo-Advisory activities (“**Robo-Advisory Rules**”). Robo-Advisors provide automated financial management services utilising information on the financial state and goals of investors. The Robo-Advisory Rules seek to regulate Robo-Advisors who operate digital investment platforms that offer financial management services by proposing that: (i) Robo-Advisors comply with extant laws and regulations applicable to financial advisors regulated by the SEC; (ii) the principal officers of Robo-Advisors have the required experience and skill in financial management and technology; (iii) mechanics be put in place to mitigate investor risks where Robo-Advisors are advising on trading in foreign securities; and (iv) material information be disclosed to investors. Robo-Advisors must continue to meet the business conduct requirements under the ISA 2025.

Artificial Intelligence (“**AI**”) has become an integral part of how Fintechs enhance their service delivery and operational efficiency. Among surveyed companies, 87.5% deploy AI-driven tools to detect and prevent fraudulent transactions, reflecting the technology’s growing role in safeguarding financial systems. Meanwhile, 62.5% leverage AI-powered chatbots and customer support solutions to manage user complaints, resolve transaction issues, and respond to routine enquiries, significantly reducing response times and improving the overall customer experience. A further 37.5% apply AI to credit assessment and lending decisions, enabling more data-driven and efficient evaluation of borrower risk profiles.[[xxxvi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn36)

### **Blockchain and digital currencies**

The ISA 2025 formally recognises digital and virtual assets, including cryptocurrencies and tokens, by expanding the definition of securities to encompass these assets and bring them under the regulatory oversight of the SEC.[[xxxvii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn37) It is important to note that the definition of “virtual assets” excludes national currencies, electronic money licensed by the CBN, utility tokens, and tokenised versions of assets. The ISA 2025 also requires all virtual assets service providers (“**VASPs**”) and exchanges to register with the SEC. The ISA 2025 also broadened the definition of a “securities exchange” to include platforms that facilitate the trading of virtual assets.[[xxxviii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn38)

Although the ISA 2025 is the principal legislation on digital and virtual assets, the SEC has issued granular rules to regulate the business of digital and virtual assets in Nigeria. The SEC issued the Rules on Issuance, Offering Platforms and Custody of Digital Assets, 2022 (“**Digital Assets Rules**”) and Exposure of Amendments to the Rules on Digital Assets Issuance, Offering Platform, Exchange and Custody, 2024 (“**Amended Digital Assets Rules**”). The Digital Assets Rules set out the registration requirements for various digital assets undertakings such as digital assets offering platforms, digital asset custodians, and digital assets exchange (“**DAX**”). The Amended Digital Assets Rules added a new licence category known as the Digital Assets Intermediary and created new sub-categories under the DAX licence that are a Digital Assets Over-the-Counter Exchange or a Digital Broker Model. It should be noted that, in practice, the SEC continues to rely on the Amended Digital Assets Rules.

The SEC’s Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Program (“**ARIP**”) Framework, introduced in June 2024, provides a structured onboarding pathway for VASPs and Digital Investment Service Providers seeking to operate in Nigeria’s capital markets, offering a six-month Approval-In-Principle period during which applicants must demonstrate regulatory compliance. So far, the SEC has granted approval in principle to two digital asset exchanges, Busha Digital Limited and Quidax Technologies Limited, allowing them to commence operations under the ARIP Framework.[[xxxix]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn39)

Additionally, the CBN has permitted financial institutions to open designated accounts for digital assets service providers, provide designated settlement accounts and settlement services and act as channels for foreign exchange flows and trade under the Guidelines on Operations of Bank Accounts for Virtual Assets Service Providers, 2023 (“**VASP Guidelines**”),[[xl]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn40) and this has led to an increase in participation in the sector. By 2025, around 10.3% of Nigerians held cryptocurrency.[[xli]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn41)

From January 1, 2026, virtual assets are now subject to taxes and VASPs are required to register with the Nigerian Revenue Authority.[[xlii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn42)

## **Regulatory and insurance technology**

Traditional financial institutions and Fintechs continue to face evolving regulatory obligations and reporting requirements. Regulatory technology (“**Regtech**”) facilitates the automation of compliance processes to enable Fintechs to mitigate cybersecurity risks and meet compliance requirements. In response to rising digital fraud and technological breaches in Nigeria, the CBN issued a circular on March 10, 2026, mandating banks, payment service providers, and other financial institutions to deploy Anti-Money Laundering (“**AML**”) systems. This directive, alongside key legislative developments, has further shaped and strengthened the Regtech landscape in Nigeria. Similarly, the implementation of the General Application and Implementation Directive, 2025 (“**GAID**”) is expected to impact financial institutions by reinforcing data protection standards and enhancing compliance requirements. Regtech continues to gain traction in regulatory reporting and compliance, KYC processes, and fraud detection and prevention tools. Recently, on April 20, 2026, the Nigerian Communications Commission (“**NCC**”) launched the Telecoms Identity Risk Management System Portal, a tool designed to curb SIM-enabled fraud by aggregating data on recycled and flagged phone numbers. The portal provides financial service providers with visibility into the status of phone numbers, a key identifier widely used in the financial sector.[[xliii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn43) The Nigerian Regtech industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of 19.3% from 2024 through to 2029, reaching $507.2 million by the end of 2029.[[xliv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn44)

Insurance technology (“**Insurtech**”) explores and expands the relationship between insurance products/services and technology. The insurance space continues to undergo significant regulatory and policy improvements, particularly in relation to Insurtech. On August 5, 2025, Nigeria enacted the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (“**NIIRA**”), which provides a comprehensive legal framework for insurance in Nigeria and repeals the Insurance Act and other extant insurance legislation. The NIIRA revises the minimum capital requirements for life insurance, non-life insurance, composite insurance, and reinsurance companies, and provided the regulatory foundation for Insurtech operations.

In furtherance of this evolving landscape, the National Insurance Commission (“**NAICOM**”) issued the Guidelines for Insurtech Operations in Nigeria on August 1, 2025. The Guidelines stipulate the types of services that Partnering and Standalone Insurtechs can offer and the application criteria for licensing. Overall, these reforms signal a clear effort to encourage innovation in the insurance sector and facilitate the growth of Insurtech.

## **Regulatory bodies**

The regulators of Fintech in Nigeria continue to cut across various sectors in Nigeria. The apex regulatory bodies of the Fintech sector in Nigeria include the CBN, the Nigerian Deposit Insurance Corporation (“**NDIC**”), the SEC, the NCC, the NAICOM, the FCCPC, the Corporate Affairs Commission (“**CAC**”), the Nigeria Revenue Service, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (“**NDPC**”), the National Office for Technology Acquisition and Promotion (“**NOTAP**”) and the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (“**ARCON**”). The extent of each regulator’s supervision will mostly depend on the transactions or services that the Fintech company is engaging in.

### **The CBN**

The CBN is the principal regulator mandated to issue licences to banks and other financial institutions. By virtue of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, 2020 (“**BOFIA**”) and the Central Bank of Nigeria Act, 2007, the CBN is able to issue the requisite licences and regulations for the sector. Fintech companies offering financial services to Nigerian consumers must obtain the appropriate licences from the CBN and comply with the CBN’s applicable guidelines.

### **The NDIC**

The NDIC is responsible for insuring all deposit liabilities of licensed banks and other deposit-receiving financial institutions in Nigeria. Fintech companies that provide mobile banking services, including deposit accounts such as checking and savings accounts for Nigerian consumers, are required to insure their deposits with the NDIC. This is pursuant to section 15 of the NDIC Act, 2023.

### **The SEC**

The SEC is the securities and capital markets regulator in Nigeria pursuant to ISA 2025. Fintech companies desirous of raising capital from the capital market must register their securities with the SEC and comply with the ISA 2025 and the rules made thereunder. Further to the Digital Assets Rules issued by the SEC in December 2022, the SEC has provided further guidance by issuing the ARIP Framework, which provides an incubation programme for all pending applications for VASP licences with the SEC. The newly enacted ISA 2025 also mandates the registration of digital assets and digital asset exchanges with the SEC.

### **The CAC**

The CAC is the regulatory body responsible for the incorporation and statutory supervision of all companies in Nigeria. The CAC makes regulations for the operation of Companies in Nigeria and ensures compliance with the statutory requirement for companies in Nigeria. Fintech companies (including banks) must be incorporated at the CAC to carry on business in (as distinct from doing business with) Nigeria except otherwise exempted from this requirement by the Minister of Trade, Industry and Investment (see sections 78 and 80 of the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020 (as amended) (“**CAMA**”)). More recently, the CAC also mandated the registration of POS terminal operators’ businesses with the CAC.[[xlv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn45)

### **The NCC**

The NCC is empowered by the Nigerian Communications Act, 2003 to regulate the telecommunications industry in Nigeria. Thus, Fintech companies offering services that involve the use of mobile networks or mobile phones are subject to NCC’s regulatory purview and must obtain operating licences from the NCC. For instance, companies that operate mobile payments must be licensed by the NCC pursuant to the Licence Framework for Value-Added Service, 2011 (“**VAS**”). The NCC VAS regulation defines a “VAS provider” as a person or organisation engaged in the provision of value-added mobile/fixed services.

### **The NDPC**

The Nigeria Data Protection Act (“**NDPA**”) is the primary legislation on data protection in Nigeria. The NDPA established the NDPC as a body that will regulate the processing of personal data by data controllers and data processors in Nigeria. In March 2025, the NDPC issued the NDPA GAID to serve as a guideline for the implementation of the NDPA in Nigeria. The GAID became effective on September 19, 2025. The NDPC’s mandate extends to Fintech companies that are handling, processing, storing or transferring the personal data of data subjects in Nigeria. Some of the key compliance obligations for Fintech entities include registration as data controllers/processors of major importance and the annual filing of data protection audit reports with the NDPC. Fintech companies carrying out cross-border personal data transfers are obligated to ensure adequate protection for such data and ensure that adequate transfer mechanisms, such as adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, or the informed consent of its data subjects, are implemented.[[xlvi]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn46)

### **The NAICOM**

The NAICOM was established by the NAICOM Act, 1997, with the responsibility for ensuring the administration, regulation, and control of insurance business in Nigeria. The NAICOM issued the Insurance Web Aggregators Operational Guidelines in 2022 to provide a framework for web aggregators. The Guidelines makes mandatory the obtention of licences before operations and rules regarding the conduct of business of these aggregators. Thus, where an Insurtech company carries on insurance business, it will require a licence from the NAICOM.

### **The FCCPC**

The FCCPC was established by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act, 2018 (“**FCCPA**”). The FCCPA prohibits anti-competitive practices in the Fintech space. The practices covered include price-fixing market division and exclusive dealing agreements that have an anti-competitive effect. It is, however, worthy to note that the regulatory oversight of the FCCPC will only extend to Fintech companies that do not qualify as banks or other financial institutions as defined by BOFIA. This is pursuant to the ever-rising arguments on who has the ultimate powers to regulate the banks and other financial institutions. While the FCCPA attempts to override other laws in competition and consumer protection matters, the BOFIA expressly excludes banking functions, financial products, and services of CBN-licensed institutions from the application of the FCCPA.[[xlvii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn47) Recently, the Federal High Court held that the FCCPC was the proper agency empowered to investigate consumer complaints involving banks and other financial institutions.[[xlviii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn48)

### **The NOTAP**

The NOTAP is an agency under the Federal Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology in Nigeria, established by the NOTAP Act, 1979. NOTAP is saddled with the responsibility of regulating and promoting the acquisition, transfer, and domestication of foreign technology in Nigeria. NOTAP’s regulation will apply to Nigerian Fintech companies that engage in technology acquisition activities and enter into technology transfer agreements in their business with foreign entities.

### **The ARCON**

The ARCON, established under the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria Act, 2022 (“**ARCON Act**”), has the exclusive power to administer, monitor and enforce compliance on matters relating to advertisements, advertising and marketing communication in Nigeria.[[xlix]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn49) Advertising is integral to building and promoting a Fintech product in Nigeria, and non-compliance with the provisions of the ARCON Act will expose Fintechs to regulatory sanctions and penalties.

## **Key regulations and regulatory approaches**

The CBN, as a major regulator for Fintech in Nigeria, has issued the following guidelines for their operations.

The regulation of Fintech in Nigeria operates within a multi-layered regulatory architecture, whereby oversight is distributed across several competent authorities depending on the nature of the activity or service being provided. Rather than a single, unified statutory framework, the Nigerian Fintech regulatory landscape is characterised by the concurrent application of sector-specific guidelines, institutional regulations, and general commercial legislation.

### **The CBN**

As the primary regulator of Fintech activities in Nigeria, the CBN has issued an extensive body of guidelines governing payment systems, digital financial services, foreign exchange, cybersecurity, and related matters. The principal instruments include, in reverse chronological order:

### **The SEC**

The SEC exercises regulatory oversight over Fintech activities that intersect with capital markets, digital assets, and investment services. The relevant instruments issued by the SEC include:

- Amended Digital Assets Rules, 2024.
- Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme Framework for the Onboarding of Virtual Assets Service Providers, 2024.
- Digital Assets Rules, 2022.
- Virtual Assets Service Provider Rules, 2022.
- Rules on Robo Advisory Services, 2021.

The SEC also strictly applies the provisions of the ISA 2025, which applies to various Fintech offerings in Nigeria.

### **Other applicable legislation and regulations**

Beyond the CBN and SEC frameworks, a broad range of federal statutes and sector-specific regulations govern various aspects of Fintech operations in Nigeria. These include:

#### *Capital markets and corporate governance*

- Investments and Securities Act, 2025.
- CAMA, 2020.
- Nigerian Exchange Technology Board Listing Rules, 2022.
- Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria Act, 2011.

#### *Digital lending and consumer protection*

- DEON Regulations, 2025.

### *Virtual assets and innovation*

### *Insurance and telecommunications*

- Insurance Web Aggregators Operational Guidelines, 2022.
- The ARCON Act, 2022.

- Nigerian Communications Act, 2003.

### *AML, financial crime and cybersecurity*

- Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, Etc.) (Amendment) Act, 2024.

- Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (Establishment, Etc.) Act, 2004.

### *Data protection*

- NDPA, 2023.

The foregoing analysis reveals a regulatory environment that is both expansive and fragmented. While several of the frameworks outlined above operate concurrently and in a complementary manner, the absence of a single, overarching Fintech statute means that regulatory applicability remains largely transaction-specific and activity-driven. This has, at times, given rise to jurisdictional ambiguity and compliance complexity for industry participants.

Ongoing consultations between regulators and industry stakeholders reflect an acknowledged need for greater coherence and harmonisation within the Nigerian Fintech regulatory ecosystem. While progress towards a more unified framework has been incremental, there is cautious optimism within the industry that a consolidated regulatory approach will materialise in the near to medium term. Recently, the Nigerian House of Representatives has moved to establish a Fintech regulatory commission.[[l]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn50)

## **Restrictions**

The Nigerian Fintech sector, while experiencing remarkable growth, operates within an increasingly restrictive regulatory environment. Fintechs must obtain the multiple licences and regulatory approvals before commencing operations. The failure of which attracts sanctions and penalties from the relevant regulatory authority, including fines, suspension of operations, or revocation of licences. While there are provided incentives and pre-launch programmes, there are certain forbidden activities that cannot be undertaken by Fintechs depending on their licensed category.

On the licensing and market entry front, banks and Fintechs are barred from obtaining new IMTO licences, limiting their remittance market participation to an agency role, while VASPs and Digital Investment Service Providers must navigate the SEC’s ARIP Framework before commencing full operations. Digital lenders face active enforcement under the DEON Regulations, with non-compliant operators being removed from the register and restricted through app stores and payment providers. In the capital markets space, crowdfunding platforms may only invite public participation with the SEC’s prior written consent, and digital assets and exchanges must be registered with the SEC under the ISA 2025. On the foreign exchange side, all IMTOs are now required to maintain naira-denominated settlement accounts with authorised dealer banks, tightening oversight of remittance flows.

Data compliance obligations add another layer of restriction, with Fintechs required to register with the NDPC, file annual audit reports, and implement strict safeguards for cross-border data transfers. Sector-specific restrictions further apply to Insurtech operators, mobile network-dependent Fintechs, and those engaged in foreign technology acquisition. Perhaps most significantly, the absence of a single overarching Fintech statute has produced a fragmented, multi-regulator approach that creates jurisdictional ambiguity and substantial compliance complexity, particularly for smaller and newer market entrants.

## **Cross-border business**

Fintech continues to transform the cross-border business in Nigeria and position it as one of Africa’s leading digital finance hubs. Fintech innovations, like real-time payments, mobile money, agency banking, and digital lending, now account for a substantial share of electronic transactions and have significantly deepened financial inclusion, expanded access to credit, and improved efficiency across the financial system.[[li]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn51)

In the cross-border context, Fintech has reduced longstanding inefficiencies in international payments, with platforms such as PAPSS enabling real-time, local-currency settlement across more than 19 African countries, thereby facilitating intra-African trade and remittances. Nigeria’s active participation in PAPSS, alongside reforms to simplify KYC requirements for low-value cross-border transactions, reflects a deliberate policy effort to lower barriers for MSMEs and enhance regional economic integration.[[lii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn52)

The CBN expanded its regulatory sandbox to cover cross-border payments, AI, and embedded finances.[[liii]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn53) Nigeria has also engaged with international bodies such as the International Monetary Fund, World Bank, and G-24 in advancing reforms for cross-border payment systems, strengthening AML/Counter-Financing of Terrorism compliance in line with Financial Action Task Force standards, and promoting a more resilient global financial architecture.[[liv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn54) The CBN’s *Policy Insight Series 2025* outlined innovation policy, inclusion, and systemic risk oversight, and also proposed initiatives such as regulatory harmonisation efforts and proposed licence recognition frameworks with other African jurisdictions (including Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa). This signals a shift towards regulatory convergence and “passporting” models to support Fintech scalability across borders.[[lv]](https://www.globallegalinsights.com/practice-areas/fintech-laws-and-regulations/nigeria/#_edn55) The CBN introduced the Foreign Exchange Code on January 28, 2025 to improve transparency and set clear rules for foreign exchange transactions.
